newsitem.title: INDIA: Mixed fortunes seen for two Indian cement majors.
newsitem.headline: Mixed fortunes seen for two Indian cement majors.

text.p: India's largest cement maker Associated Cement Companies will see a slowdown in profit growth for the first half of 1996/97, analysts said on Friday.
ACC's margins are being squeezed by cost escalation on various fronts at a time when the industry is not able to pass on cost increases to customers, they said.
"Costs have escalated by about nine rupees per 50 kg bag," said Sriram Jitendra, analyst at Classic Share & Stock Broking Services Ltd in Bombay.
Cost of almost all inputs -- fuel, transportation and power -- have gone up in recent months, affecting the entire industry.
"Barring southern India, they (company) have not been able to pass on cost increases," Jitendra said.
A Reuter poll of leading securities firms this week forecast that ACC will see a 6.1 percent drop in net profit at 1.18 billion rupees for the first half of 1996/97 (April-March).
The consensus for first half net sales was 11.6 billion rupees, showing a 3.9 percent rise over year-ago period.

Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd, ACC's rival in western and northern markets, is expected to post a 94.2 percent rise in net profit to 795.8 million rupees, and a sales increase of 55.9 percent at 4.2 billion rupees, according to the poll.

"The difference is mainly because of volumes," said Pradeep Mahtani, cement analyst at Jardine Fleming India Broking. Gujarat Ambuja commissioned a new 1.5 million plant in Himachal Pradesh but ACC had little volume increase during the period.
Mahtani said Gujarat Ambuja also benefited from higher than average cement prices in the northern Punjab state and low power and transportation costs incurred by its Himachal plant.
Gujarat Ambuja would fare well, but the poll consensus appear to be exaggerated, Sriram Jitendra of Classic Share said.
He said most analysts appear not to have accounted for tax outgoings. Gujarat Ambuja would have to pay tax according to a new minimum alternate tax (MAT) imposed in the 1996/97 bydget.

The government later exempted firms which have plants in notified backward areas from MAT. Gujarat Ambuja officials said the firm would be exempt from MAT on this account, but some analysts are not sure this would happen.
